title: Helstrom geometry with time-dependent spectral calibration
abstract: In a recent work we introduced a finite scalar-qubit-scalar spectral triple whose Connes distance reproduces the Bloch-ball trace metric up to a factor $2/Λ$, where $Λ^2=μ_L^2+μ_R^2$ for isotropic link strengths $μ_L,μ_R$ appearing in the proposed Dirac operator. Here we analyse time-dependent variation of these links, independent of the qubit dynamics. In doing so, we separate the distinguishability and calibration contributions to the spectral rate. A depolarizing example demonstrates spectral growth despite a monotonic contraction of the trace-distance. More generally, we characterize the admissible trace-distance histories compatible with a given positive spectral record and exhibit contracting and reviving realizations. At fixed $Λ$, we also study a sinusoidal link imbalance that preserves the Dirac spectrum and qubit metric, while the scalar-scalar distance oscillates with half the period of the imbalance.
summary: This work investigates the geometric relationship between the trace distance and the Connes spectral distance for evolving quantum states. By modeling the system using a spectral triple with time-dependent links, the authors show that the spectral record does not uniquely determine the trace distance history. This has implications for understanding quantum information flow and distinguishing between different physical processes.
main_problem: The paper analyzes the relationship between two measures of quantum distinguishability—the trace distance (Helstrom distance) and the Connes spectral distance—when the underlying spectral calibration factor is time-dependent.
main_result: It demonstrates that the spectral distance growth can occur even when the trace distance contracts, showing that the spectral record alone is insufficient to determine the true history of quantum state distinguishability.
method: The authors utilize a finite spectral triple structure to model qubit evolution, deriving relationships between the time derivatives of the spectral distance, trace distance, and the time-dependent calibration factor $\Lambda(t)$.
model_or_system: The model involves qubit states evolving under time-dependent quantum channels, geometrically embedded within a spectral triple structure containing a qubit block and two scalar blocks connected by time-dependent links.
key_observables: Trace distance $T(t)$, Connes spectral distance $d(t)$, and the calibration factor $\Lambda(t)$.
important_parameters: Link strengths ($\mu_L, \mu_R$), the imbalance parameter $ eta$, and the decay rate $\gamma$ (in depolarizing examples).
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on the spectral triple formalism and assumes the validity of the derived relationships between the three distinguishability measures.
figures_summary: Figure 1 illustrates the geometry relating the spectral distance to the Bloch-ball trace metric. Figure 2 illustrates the evolution, showing spectral distance peaking while trace distance decreases under depolarization, and also shows the scalar-scalar distance for an oscillating link imbalance.
paper_structure: The paper first establishes the relationship between the spectral and trace distances using the spectral triple. It then analyzes the time evolution by separating the distinguishability and calibration contributions. Finally, it explores the ambiguity by showing that different physical histories can yield the same spectral record, which can be resolved by analyzing the scalar radii.
why_interesting: It provides a rigorous geometric framework for understanding how different mathematical measures of quantum distinguishability relate under time evolution, which is crucial for characterizing open quantum systems.

The scalar states ωL and ωR lie at distances ℓL = µ−1 L and ℓR = µ−1 R from every qubit state, with dD(ωL, ωR)2 = ℓ2 L + ℓ2 R.
